proof:
# Every zero-right-index double knot has deficit below one sixth

## Theorem and scope

Let d>=2 and 1<=H<=d be integers. Put

    t=1/(d+1),  Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d,
    a=t(1+1/H),  beta=t/d,
    W_H=sum_{j>=0}(1-aj)_+^d,
    K_H=sum_{j=0}^{H-1}(1-j/d)^(d-1)(1-j/H).

Every summation index in this note is an integer, and x_+=max{x,0}.
Then

    W_H-K_H < 1/6.                                    (1)

At precisely the J=0 double knots from
`candidate a38c69b78fd106d1`, the
normalized diagonal-envelope deficit is D/Gamma=W_H-K_H. Thus (1)
closes the entire J=0 family at the uniform sufficient bound
D<Gamma/6. This is an arithmetic kernel theorem, not an assertion
of a mixed-integer center theorem.

For completeness, the normalization follows directly. For h>=0,
set r_h=1-ah, q_h=t-beta h, and p_h=t+beta(h+1). On positive-radius
terms one has

    r_h-dq_h=t(1-h/H),
    r_h-dp_h=-h(a+t)<=0.

Since d^d t^d=Gamma and q_h=t(1-h/d), the normalized left envelope
is (1-h/d)^(d-1)(1-h/H) for 0<=h<H, and is zero otherwise. The right
envelope is zero. This gives the asserted identity without a
limiting argument or an omitted endpoint contribution.

## 1. Elementary geometric-sum bound

For 0<a<=1, Bernoulli's inequality gives

    (1-aj)_+ <= (1-a)^j       for every integer j>=0.

Consequently, for any positive integer d, with q=(1-a)^d<1,

    sum_{j>=0}(1-aj)_+^d <= 1/(1-q).                  (2)

All sums on the left are finite. The infinite geometric sum on the
right is used only as a convergent bound.

We will use 8/3<e<3 and e^2>7. These follow directly from the
positive exponential series: the first four terms of e sum to 8/3;
the bound m!>=2^(m-1) for m>=1 gives e<3, with strictness for m>=3;
and the terms through degree four in the series for e^2 sum to 7.
Also log 2>2/3, because

    log 2=2 integral_0^(1/3) (1-s^2)^(-1) ds > 2/3.

## 2. Three monotonicity facts

### 2.1. The mass ratio decreases with dimension

Fix an integer H>=2, and let c=1+1/H. For real z>=H define

    Q_H(z)=(1-c/(z+1))^z.

Then Q_H is strictly decreasing. Indeed set x=c/(z+1), so
0<x<=1/H. The logarithmic derivative of Q_H is

    log(1-x)+x/(1-x)-x^2/[c(1-x)].                    (3)

Define

    A(x)=[x+(1-x)log(1-x)]/x^2
        =sum_{m>=2} x^(m-2)/[m(m-1)].

The equality follows from the absolutely convergent logarithm
series for 0<x<1. Equation (3) is

    x^2/(1-x) * [A(x)-1/c].                          (4)

The positive series shows that A increases on (0,1). If H>=3,

    A(x) < 1/[2(1-x)]
         <= H/[2(H-1)] <= H/(H+1)=1/c.

The first inequality is strict because the series coefficients
1/[m(m-1)] are strictly less than 1/2 for m>=3 and x>0. If H=2,

    A(x)<=A(1/2)=2-2 log 2 < 2/3=1/c.

Thus (4) is strictly negative in all cases. In particular, when
d>=H,

    (1-(1+1/H)/(d+1))^d <= (1-1/H)^H=:q_H.            (5)

Combining (2) and (5) gives W_H<=1/(1-q_H).

### 2.2. Noninitial kernel coefficients increase with dimension

Fix an integer j>=2. For real z>j, the function

    B_j(z)=(1-j/z)^(z-1)

is strictly increasing. With x=j/z in (0,1), its logarithmic
derivative is

    log(1-x)+x/(1-x)-x^2/[j(1-x)]
      =sum_{m>=2} [(m-1)/m-1/j] x^m >=0.              (6)

Every coefficient is nonnegative because j>=2; a coefficient for
m>=3 is positive, so the derivative is strictly positive. Hence
for 2<=j<=H-1 and d>=H,

    (1-j/d)^(d-1)(1-j/H) >= (1-j/H)^H.                (7)

For j=1, the elementary inequality log(1+y)<y for y>0 gives
(1+1/(d-1))^(d-1)<e, and therefore

    (1-1/d)^(d-1)>1/e>1/3.                           (8)

In particular, whenever H>=2,

    K_H > 1+(H-1)/(3H)
              +sum_{j=2}^{H-1}(1-j/H)^H.             (9)

An empty sum is zero.

### 2.3. Fixed-index power terms increase with the chain length

For a fixed positive integer j and real z>j, the function
(1-j/z)^z is strictly increasing: putting x=j/z, its logarithmic
derivative is

    log(1-x)+x/(1-x)
      =sum_{m>=2}(m-1)x^m/m>0.                       (10)

This will be used only for j=2,3 and z>=10.

## 3. The single-knot case H=1

Here K_1=1 and a=2/(d+1). Put
q=((d-1)/(d+1))^d. The integral identity

    log((1+x)/(1-x))=2 integral_0^x (1-s^2)^(-1) ds

with x=1/d shows log((d+1)/(d-1))>2/d. Thus q<e^(-2)<1/7, and (2)
yields

    W_1-K_1 <= q/(1-q)<1/6.                          (11)

This argument includes d=2 and requires no asymptotic estimate.

## 4. The eight remaining small chain lengths

For 2<=H<=9, define the explicit rational number

    U_H = 1/[1-(1-1/H)^H]
          -1-(H-1)/(3H)-sum_{j=2}^{H-1}(1-j/H)^H.

Equations (5) and (9) imply W_H-K_H<U_H. Direct rational arithmetic
gives the following complete certificate; every displayed denominator
is positive.

| H | 1/6-U_H |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0 |
| 3 | 5/1026 |
| 4 | 2717/134400 |
| 5 | 1349881/39393750 |
| 6 | 11033401/241297056 |
| 7 | 147714066079/2686102437606 |
| 8 | 11558430263869/184757665136640 |
| 9 | 13502918255940587/196191874965540258 |

The entries are obtained merely by substituting the indicated H in
the preceding finite rational expression. They may equivalently be
verified by cross multiplication of its positive denominators. In
particular U_H<=1/6, and the strict inequality from (9) proves (1)
even for H=2, where this coarser rational certificate has zero margin.

## 5. Every chain length H>=10

The inequality log(1-x)<-x gives
q_H=(1-1/H)^H<1/e<3/8. Thus (2) and (5) give

    W_H < 8/5.                                      (12)

Retain only the four terms j=0,1,2,3 in K_H. Equations (7)--(10),
together with (H-1)/(3H)>=3/10, give

    K_H > 13/10+(4/5)^10+(7/10)^10.                  (13)

Subtracting (13) from (12) gives

    W_H-K_H
      < 8/5-13/10-(4/5)^10-(7/10)^10
      = 1643782927/10000000000
      = 1/6-68651219/30000000000 < 1/6.               (14)

Sections 3--5 exhaust every pair of integers d>=2 and 1<=H<=d,
and prove the theorem.

## Verification and limitations

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_zero_right_index_knot_one_sixth_minkowski.py` checks the
finite rational certificate, normalization identities, the large-H
constant, and many exact instances of the algebraic comparisons.
The proof for arbitrary dimension is the displayed calculus and
inequalities, not those sampled checks.

No continuity argument in d, interchange of an infinite sum with a
limit, or presumed extremal index is used. Real z occurs only to
prove elementary monotonicity of explicit positive scalar functions.
The original deficits and all knot indices remain discrete.
